extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and government; scholars and policymakers interested in foundations of legitimate authority
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of criteria for legitimate political authority and the ends and limits of government, including the basis of consent, the purposes of society, defects of the state of nature, forms of commonwealth, and limits on legislative power. Useful as a theoretical baseline for evaluating claims about rightful authority, obligations of subjects, and proper scope of lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent as basis of political society
rubrics_metrics.description: “the beginning of politic society depends upon the consent of the individuals, to join into, and make one society”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals must consent to unite and form a commonwealth; this consent is the origin of legitimate government and allows the society to set up whatever form of government it thinks fit. Historical forms do not prove natural divine rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of government derive from placement of legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: “the form of the government is a perfect democracy… or … an oligarchy: or else … a monarchy”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form (democracy, oligarchy, monarchy, hereditary/elective, or mixed) depends on who holds the supreme legislative power. Communities may reassign the supreme power and thereby constitute a new form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of monarchy often due to war-leadership needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Early societies commonly chose one ruler because they needed a single commander to defend them in war; kings often functioned chiefly as captains or generals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monarchy’s prevalence in early polities is explained by practical needs (defence, simplicity, familiarity with paternal authority), not by parental or divine right. Examples include judges/kings in Israel whose chief role was military leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between express and tacit consent
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a common distinction of an express and a tacit consent; express consent clearly admits a man into society; the difficulty is what to regard as tacit consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express consent (explicit agreement) makes one a full member and generally binds perpetually. Tacit consent requires careful delimitation (see possession/enjoyment criteria) and binds only to the extent of that tacit engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession or enjoyment under a government constitutes tacit consent
rubrics_metrics.description: “every man, that hath any possessions, or enjoyment, of any part of the dominions of any government, doth thereby give his tacit consent, and is as far forth obliged to obedience to the laws of that government, during such enjoyment”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possessions (land held forever, lodging for a week, or travelling on the highway) imply tacit consent to obey laws while enjoying those protections. The obligation begins and ends with the enjoyment; one may quit the enjoyment (by sale, donation, departure) and so end the tacit obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annexation of possessions when incorporating into a commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man incorporates himself into any commonwealth, he unites his possessions to the community and they become subject to that government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entering a society binds both person and possessions; it would contradict joining for property security to claim possessions exempt from the community’s jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residence or temporary protection does not equal membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting to the laws of any country and enjoying privileges and protection makes not a man a member of that society; this is only a local protection and homage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreigners who live under another government and enjoy its protections are bound to obey it while under its protection, but are not thereby permanent members or subjects unless they make explicit engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: A child is not bound to a government by a father's consent
rubrics_metrics.description: A child is born a subject of no country or government; parental submission cannot bind the son or posterity to perpetual subjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children are under parental authority until age of discretion; on attaining maturity they are free to choose what government to join. Examples: nationality by birth abroad does not automatically make the child a subject of the father's sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary end of political society: preservation of property (life, liberty, estate)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the great and chief end… of men’s uniting into commonwealths… is the preservation of their property” (understood as lives, liberties, and estates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hazards of the state of nature—uncertainty and invasion—motivate men to join society to secure their possessions and safety. No rational agent would enter society to make his condition worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three defects of the state of nature that government must remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature there wants: (1) an established, known law; (2) a known and indifferent judge; (3) power to execute the sentence when right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures and governments exist to provide these instruments—clear laws, impartial adjudication, and effective enforcement—so individuals can enjoy property and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers individuals give up on entering society
rubrics_metrics.description: On joining a political society, a man gives up (1) the unrestricted liberty to do whatever he thinks fit for preservation, and (2) the private power to punish; these are transferred to society’s laws and executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first power is regulated by laws for the common good; the second (punishment) is entrusted to the society’s appointed executors and limited by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature must govern by established, promulgated, standing laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative is obliged to govern by established standing laws, promulgated and known to the people, and not by extemporary decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should be visible so citizens can know their duties and the penalties for transgression; ad hoc decrees undermine predictability and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for indifferent and upright judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes must be decided by indifferent and upright judges, who apply the laws to controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartial adjudication is essential to prevent partiality, revenge, or negligence that afflict the state of nature; judges must apply established laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force limited to law execution and defence
rubrics_metrics.description: The community’s force should be employed at home only in the execution of laws, and abroad to prevent or redress foreign injuries, directed to the peace, safety, and public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government force is not a general license but is justified only to execute established laws and to protect the community; it must serve public ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative is supreme but its power is limited by natural law/public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the legislative is the supreme power, it is not absolutely arbitrary: 'it can be no more than those persons had in a state of nature' and 'their power... is limited to the public good of the society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No legislature may lawfully destroy, enslave, or impoverish the people; human laws must conform to the law of nature (preservation of mankind) and cannot validly contravene it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human laws invalid if contrary to the law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules that legislators make must be conformable to the law of nature, i.e. to the will of God, of which that is a declaration; 'no human sanction can be good, or valid against it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation that violates the fundamental natural law (preservation of society and mankind) lacks moral and legal validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative authority requires society’s consent and is the source of lawfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative is the supreme power and laws have no force unless sanctioned by the legislative which the public has chosen and appointed; 'without this the law could not have… the consent of the society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edicts from sources without the society’s sanction (foreign powers or unauthorized bodies) are mere tyranny and lack the binding force of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express consent creates perpetual membership; tacit consent is conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: One who has by actual agreement and any express declaration given his consent to be of any commonwealth is perpetually and indispensably obliged to be a subject; tacit consent (from mere enjoyment) binds only while the enjoyment continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressly entering a society generally precludes returning to the state of nature except if the government dissolves or a public act severs membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of restraints on sovereign power when rulers become ambitious or corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: When ambition and luxury cause rulers to retain and increase power without performing the duties for which it was given, people find it necessary 'to examine more carefully the original and rights of government' and to find ways 'to restrain the exorbitances, and prevent the abuses' of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical experience justifies institutional checks (laws, limitations, separation of powers) to prevent abuse of delegated authority.
